name: Niko

card.essence: love in plain paint: one animal, plainly seen and warmly made, glowing against a dark ground (Pirosmani painted a giraffe, deer, sows, calves, sheep). Niko is one animal, never a herd.
rhymes: one animal, frontal or in profile, set large in its field and looking out
leave: the giraffe itself: the long neck and spotted coat
the crescent and stars on its shoulder
the cream-on-black oilcloth look, which is Pirosmani's own manner and must not appear before him

step0.title: Niko, as he is
step0.medium: Cream and ochre oil paint on black oilcloth, the black showing through as the animal's patches (today's giraffe, painted as Pirosmani painted animals)

steps.title: after the itinerant signboard painters of Tiflis
steps.medium: Oil paint on sheet tin: a tavern or shop signboard
steps.link: Pirosmani is said to have learned painting bit by bit from itinerant artists who painted shop and dukhan (tavern) signs, then ran a decorative-painting workshop (signs) with Zaziashvili from the mid-1880s.
steps.source: ru.wikipedia, Пиросмани: «Понемногу учился живописи у странствующих художников, расписывавших вывески лавок и духанов.» (He gradually learned painting from itinerant artists who painted shop and dukhan signboards; translation mine). Also Apchinskaya, Tretyakov Gallery Magazine 1/2009: in the late 19th century he worked in Tiflis taverns 'creating sign-boards, oil paintings, murals and glass paintings'.
steps.native: A Tiflis shop or dukhan signboard of the 1880s: oil paint on a sheet of tin, the thing on offer (a bull, a lamb, a fish) drawn large, flat and frontal in a few strong colours on a bright flat ground of blue, red or ochre, with a painted border and a band for lettering (a blur of Georgian and Russian letters, never legible). Hard-wearing, quickly painted, a little rusted at the edges. Keep it clearly a trade sign on tin, not a black oilcloth picture.

steps.title: after late-medieval Georgian church painting
steps.medium: Earth pigments on lime plaster: a church wall painting
steps.link: The Georgian National Museum's chief curator ties Pirosmani's art to late-medieval Georgian church painting and sculpture; Pirosmani himself said he was no icon painter, so this is a family likeness, not a lesson.
steps.source: Irina Arsenishvili, Pera Museum catalogue 'Pirosmani: A Legend in Naive Art': "The concept of genesis in Pirosmani's art has been put in a broader perspective: the link with the late Medieval Georgian church painting and sculpture, with the so called 'Tiflis school' of portrayal art, and with monuments of memorial character - grave reliefs." Apchinskaya (Tretyakov Gallery Magazine 1/2009): "the entire tenor of the imagery evoked Georgian medieval frescos and icons"; Pirosmani: "I was not an icon painter, I painted St. George only once."
steps.native: A Georgian church wall painting (Svaneti and Kakheti are the usual homes): ochre, red oxide, green earth, lamp-black and a deep blue ground laid flat on lime plaster, figures frontal and solemn with large calm eyes, bodies as simple coloured shapes outlined in dark paint, each scene on a plain band of colour. Its animals (the ox and ass of the Nativity, a lion, a stag) are drawn the same way: frontal or in profile, flat, still, not fussed over. A weathered wall, patches lost to damp.

steps.title: after medieval Georgian stone relief
steps.medium: Carved stone relief (limestone or tuff) on a church wall or stele
steps.kind: spiritual (tradition; scholars name church sculpture and grave reliefs)
steps.link: Arsenishvili also names church sculpture and grave reliefs among his sources; medieval Georgian relief carved the animal, above all the deer, as a sacred beast, and Pirosmani painted deer himself ('Doe against a landscape', 1913).
steps.source: Nino Goderdzishvili, dissertation (2020): "The hunting theme is one of the most important in the diverse iconographic repertoire of medieval Georgian relief sculpture", with 'the cult of the deer as a sacred animal'. Art Newspaper 25 Oct 2018, Arsenishvili: "late medieval Georgian church painting" and gravestones make him a "living bearer of the 'cultural memory' of his country".
steps.native: A medieval Georgian stone relief: one deer (or a hunter's quarry) cut in low relief on a pale limestone slab or church facade, the body a smooth flat mass with a few incised lines for eye, antlers and legs, a plain recess behind it and a rope or plaited-vine border. Weathered, lichen-tinted, no colour. The animal fills the block, patient and frontal or in profile.

note: No teacher is documented ('he never received any professional education'). The famous champions (Ilia and Kirill Zdanevich and Le-Dantyu, summer 1912; Larionov and Goncharova's Target show, 1913) came after him, so they cannot be jumps back. The English-language 'Persian/Qajar' and 'Byzantine icon' links in Apollo and Povelikhina/Kovtun are 'perhaps' claims; I left them out.
confidence: Weak throughout: none of the three is a documented hand-off. Signboards are the most solid (the trade he plainly worked in, and Russian Wikipedia's unreferenced 'itinerant painters' sentence is UNCONFIRMED beyond that); church painting and stone relief are scholars' claims about what he drew on (Arsenishvili), and the relief is the weakest.

name: Emily

card.essence: the one right word: say the most with the least. One small quiet bee carrying one pressed flower, a single careful detail doing the work of ten. Emily is one bee.
rhymes: one small bee, only where a tradition has its own (Watts's busy bee, bees in a vellum margin)
leave: the round striped body, the tiny white collar and the pressed flower held in the forelegs
the sincere-eyed pose and any character acting

step0.title: Emily, as she is
step0.medium: Ink outline and flat gouache on paper: a small cartoon-style illustration of a bee with a white collar and one pressed flower

steps.title: after Isaac Watts, as New England stitched him
steps.medium: Silk thread on linen: a New England schoolgirl's sampler carrying a verse of Watts
steps.kind: cited influence (she quotes him in her own hand)
steps.link: Dickinson's poem 'Where bells no more affright the morn' (F114, c. 1859, bound in fascicle 5) quotes Watts's hymn 'There is a land of pure delight'; her family church, First Church Amherst, sang Samuel Worcester's Watts.
steps.source: Dickinson, F114: "Oh could we climb where Moses stood, / And view the Landscape o'er" (Watts: "Could we but climb where Moses stood, / And view the landscape o'er, / Not Jordan's stream, nor death's cold flood / Should fright us from the shore."), noted by Thomas Johnson, in 'White Heat: Emily Dickinson in 1862' (Dartmouth). Poets.org: "There, as a child, the young poet was exposed to Samuel Worcester's edition of Watts's hymns, The Psalms and Spiritual Songs." Sampler: Pilgrim Hall Museum, Elizabeth Gooch (Boston, d. 1747): "It has a verse from a 1715 book called Divine Songs for Children by Rev. Isaac Watts."
steps.native: A New England girl's sampler: fine cross-stitch in silk on undyed linen, a few rows of alphabet, one short verse in stitched capitals (kept tiny and not legible), a border of strawberries or carnations, and a few small naturalistic motifs: a bird, a sheep, a flower spray, perhaps a bee. Threads faded to rose, ochre, sage and indigo, the linen gone cream. A domestic object, small, patient and exact: the verse is the whole point, the flower stitched flat.

steps.title: after Sternhold and Hopkins's metrical psalter
steps.medium: Letterpress on paper: a small metrical psalter with printed tunes
steps.date: London, 1562; this form from the 1584 edition
steps.kind: cited influence (the book Watts set out to improve)
steps.link: Watts as a boy objected to the poor poetry of Sternhold and Hopkins; his 1719 preface says their psalms made the devotion vanish, yet he kept to their few metres, so his hymns could be sung to tunes already known. Dickinson's common metre is that metre.
steps.source: Watts, preface to Psalms of David Imitated (1719), quoted by Robin Leaver, Christian History 31 (1991): "that Spirit of Devotion vanishes and is lost, the Psalm dies upon their Lips"; Watts "chose to restrict himself to the handful of meters of the old English metrical psalms". PDR: "Sternhold and Hopkins wrote almost all of their Psalms in the 'common' or ballad metre."
steps.native: An Elizabethan metrical psalter (John Day, London): a small thick book in black-letter and roman type on soft paper gone brown, each psalm a block of four-line stanzas in common metre, a short tune printed in notes on a staff above it, a woodcut-ornamented capital and a plain ruled border. A psalm is a tune and four lines, nothing more; the bee or the flower, if any, a tiny printer's ornament.

steps.title: after the medieval Psalter
steps.medium: Ink and pigment on vellum: an illuminated psalter leaf
steps.date: England, c. 1320-1340 (as in the Luttrell Psalter)
steps.kind: tradition (the text both versions rework; no documented hand-off)
steps.link: A metrical psalter is the 150 Psalms put into English rhyme; the Latin Psalter was the standard illuminated book they were sung from. Its margins are famous for small, everyday creatures and things.
steps.source: PDR: a metrical psalter is a "versified version of all 150 psalms"; Luttrell Psalter (British Library Add MS 42130), c. 1320-40, 309 vellum leaves, with "marginal pictures of saints and Bible stories, and scenes of rural life" (Wikipedia).
steps.native: A 14th-century English psalter leaf: ruled vellum with a few lines of Latin in black textura, a red-and-blue pen-flourished initial touched with gold, and in the wide margin a thin vine whose branches carry tiny quick-tinted creatures and flowers (a bee, a bird, a flower head) drawn in a few lines of ink and wash. The psalm sits small in a large margin of bare vellum; the small margin creature is as alive as the text.

note: Her own list of models (letter to Higginson, 25 April 1862: "For Poets - I have Keats - and Mr and Mrs Browning. For Prose - Mr Ruskin - Sir Thomas Browne - and the Revelations"; "my Lexicon - was my only companion") does not name Watts. His debt is real but rests on her F114 quotation, the church's hymn book and scholarship, not on a sentence of hers. Watts's famous 'How doth the little busy bee' (Divine Songs, 1715) is a coincidence of bees; I found nothing tying it to hers. A fully documented alternative line exists through that letter (Keats, then Spenser, then Chaucer: manuscript, woodcut, vellum); not researched in depth here.
confidence: Step 1 solid (her own manuscript quotes Watts), though the sampler is a stand-in for how New England met him, not something she cited. Step 2 solid (Watts's own words). Step 3 is a tradition by shared text, not a hand-off, and the weakest.

name: George

card.essence: the meaning in a movement: see the music, hear the dance. One small clear note made visible as a single turn, timed to a pulse, with nothing wasted. George is one tuning fork.
rhymes: a thin looping line (a turn, a track on the floor)
a beat kept (a count, a tune)
leave: the tuning fork and its two prongs
the blue-and-gold Ballets Russes gouache look

step0.title: George, as he is
step0.medium: Gouache and pencil on paper: a costume sketch in the Ballets Russes manner, of a small tuning fork dancing en pointe

steps.title: after Petipa's Imperial Ballet
steps.medium: Pencil on a small sheet of paper: a ballet master's working notes
steps.link: At the Imperial school Balanchine studied under Pavel Gerdt, Petipa's premier danseur, and he called Ballet Imperial a tribute to Petipa as 'the father of the classical ballet'.
steps.source: Balanchine, quoted by the Balanchine Trust: "a contemporary tribute to Petipa, 'the father of the classical ballet,' and to Tschaikovsky, his greatest composer." Wikipedia, Pavel Gerdt: "Among his pupils at the Imperial Ballet School were Michel Fokine, Vaslav Nijinsky, Tamara Karsavina, George Balanchine, and Anna Pavlova." Object: Petipa, notes on the cat's dance in The Sleeping Beauty, pencil on paper, 15.8 x 10.3 cm, Bakhrushin Theatre Museum (КП 107324).
steps.native: A ballet master's pocket working sheet like Petipa's notes for the cat's dance in The Sleeping Beauty: soft pencil on small, folded, smudged paper, hasty ground-plans of the stage with dancers as small dots and crosses in lines, diagonals and one curling path, arrows for their movement, bar counts scribbled beside them, a few words (kept illegible), no colour. The dancers are marks; the pattern on the floor and the count are the dance. (The exact contents of the Bakhrushin sheet are UNCONFIRMED; this follows Petipa's known 'notes and sketches'.)

steps.title: after Christian Johansson's class
steps.medium: Carved and varnished wood: a small violin and a thick stick, a dancing master's tools
steps.link: Gerdt studied under Christian Johansson, the Swedish master who trained under Bournonville and partnered Marie Taglioni; in class Johansson kept the beat with a violin and a thick stick.
steps.source: Marius Petipa Society: "he was always accompanied by his violin and a thick stick that he used to keep the musical beat underneath his mumbled counts of music." Nikolai Legat, taking over his classes (quoted by Jonathan Still): "From him I acquired the very essence of his school ... even to the preference for accompanying my instruction on the violin, rather than the piano." Wikipedia, Pavel Gerdt: "Gerdt studied under Christian Johansson, Alexander Pimenov ... and with Jean-Antoine Petipa".
steps.native: A dancing master's class kit of the 1880s: a small violin of amber-brown varnished maple and spruce with a short bow, worn pale at the shoulder and fingerboard, and beside it a thick plain wooden stick for striking the time, laid on bare worn pine floorboards under cool window light. No ornament. The room is a pulse; the instrument and stick are all the music and all the instruction. (Whether Johansson's violin was a pocket 'kit' type is UNCONFIRMED.)

steps.title: after Beauchamp-Feuillet dance notation
steps.medium: Copper engraving printed in black on laid paper: a page of dance notation
steps.kind: tradition (the French school, la belle danse)
steps.link: Johansson learned in Copenhagen from Bournonville, who learned in Paris from Auguste Vestris, a line (Vestris, his father Gaetan, Dupre) back to the Paris Opera's Royal Academy; Johansson is described as trained in the French style 'la belle danse', the style Feuillet's Choregraphie records.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Christian Johansson: "trained in the French classical style, la belle danse"; Wikipedia, August Bournonville: "directed to Auguste Vestris for training" (Paris, 1824); PDR on Feuillet's Choregraphie (1701): its five positions "largely correspond to classical ballet"; Pierre Beauchamp later claimed the invention as his own.
steps.native: A page of Feuillet's Choregraphie: copper-engraved in black on cream laid paper, the dance drawn as a thin looping track down the page like a ribbon laid on the floor, with tiny step-signs like hooked and flagged notes along it, bar lines crossing the track, and the tune engraved on a staff above; plate-mark and a ruled border visible. A turn is a curl in the line; the music and the movement share one page, nothing wasted.

note: Balanchine's own 'turning point' was Stravinsky's Apollo (1928) ('the score was a revelation ... I could dare not to use everything', paraphrased; Pacific Northwest Ballet, Mariinsky), a strong cited influence. I left it out because Apollo belongs to the Ballets Russes years, the same world as today's costume-sketch drawing, so it fails the signature test.
confidence: Step 1: the Balanchine quote and the Gerdt pupil link are solid; the notebook is a stand-in for Petipa's method. Step 2: the Gerdt-Johansson teacher link is solid; the violin-and-stick detail rests on a modern society page, Wikipedia and Legat's memoir. Step 3 is weakest: a tradition by name (la belle danse) and a teacher line, with no quote showing Johansson or Bournonville used Feuillet.

name: Rikyū

card.essence: the one flower in the empty room: take things away until what is left matters, and let the empty space be part of the work. One bloom, set alone.
rhymes: a wide margin of empty space around it
leave: the small, uneven black tea bowl, tipped toward you
the morning glory on its rim
black raku glaze as a look
any 'Zen' pastiche: no imitation script, gongs or stereotyped speech (Originality's caution)

step0.title: Rikyū, as he is
step0.medium: A small, uneven, hand-built black raku-glazed earthenware tea bowl with one morning-glory bloom resting on its rim
step0.date: after Chōjirō's black bowls made for Rikyū, 1580s

steps.title: after Takeno Jōō
steps.medium: Unpainted cypress and green bamboo: a plain well-bucket used as a water jar, with a cut-bamboo lid-rest and a hand-carved bamboo scoop
steps.link: At nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, Rikyū began to study tea under Jōō; Jōō's tea turned plain household things into tea utensils, and the Omotesenke school says that view passed to Rikyū.
steps.source: Omotesenke Fushin'an: 「白木の釣瓶を水指に見立てたり、竹を削って自ら茶杓をつくったり、あるいは青竹を切って蓋置にするなど、清浄な白木の美を茶の湯に加えることに成功しました。こうした創造的な茶の見方が紹鴎の弟子千利休に伝えられ」 (He turned a plain wooden well-bucket into a water jar, carved bamboo tea scoops himself, cut green bamboo for lid-rests ... this creative way of seeing tea was passed to his disciple Sen no Rikyū; translation mine). Wikipedia: "at nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, he began to study tea under Takeno Jō'ō".
steps.native: Jōō's wabi tea: no lacquer, gold or Chinese bronze, but things from the house and the garden left plain. A well-bucket of pale unpainted cypress with its bamboo hoops and rope handle set on a tatami as the water jar; a lid-rest cut from a length of green bamboo, still glossy, its node showing; a scoop he carved himself from a slip of bamboo. One thing at a time, bare pale wood, and a great deal of empty mat; if a flower appears, one bloom in a plain bamboo section (a flower holder is not documented for Jōō himself).

steps.title: after Murata Jukō
steps.medium: Glazed stoneware: a Chinese celadon bowl of the kind named for him (Jukō celadon)
steps.date: made in Fujian, Southern Song (12th-13th c.); prized by Jukō (d. 1502)
steps.link: Jōō's first tea teacher was Fujita Sōri, then Sōshu, Jukō's heir; Rikyū is said to have taught 'the craft from Jōō, the Way from Jukō', and bought one of the four recorded Jukō bowls and used it at an early tea gathering.
steps.source: Japanese Wikipedia, 武野紹鴎: 「『山上宗二記』によれば、紹鷗の茶の湯の最初の師は藤田宗理であり、その後、その師であり珠光の「跡目」とされる宗珠の直弟子になった」; 「特に利休は「術は紹鷗、道は珠光より」と説いており」. 村田珠光: 「その四つの《珠光茶碗》のうちの一つを千利休が購入し、若かった頃の茶会で使用している」. Idemitsu Museum bowl: Murata Shuko loved this "clumsy and austere" celadon as "more suitable for tea" than refined celadon.
steps.native: A Jukō celadon bowl, about 15 cm across: Fujian folk-kiln celadon with a thick transparent glaze gone from jade-green to a warm loquat yellow-brown in an oxidising firing, grey-white body showing at the foot, the outside combed with fine 'cat-scratch' lines and the inside carved with a few free cloud shapes. A plain, slightly clumsy bowl, set alone on bare tatami or a plain tray, nothing beside it.

steps.title: after the Song tenmoku bowl
steps.medium: Iron-glazed stoneware (Jian ware) bowl on a black lacquer stand
steps.date: Fujian, Southern Song, 12th-13th c.; prized in Ashikaga Japan
steps.link: Wabi-cha grew as a move away from the fashion for costly imported Chinese wares (karamono); the tenmoku bowl, named for the Tianmu monasteries, was the prestige tea bowl. Rikyū's hand-built black bowls are its deliberate opposite.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Wabi-cha: "tea ceremony had become widespread, with a preference for expensive wares of Chinese origin known as karamono. Wabi-cha evolved as part of a movement to appreciate local wares and simpler styles." Wikipedia, Tenmoku: "Tenmoku takes its name from the Tianmu Mountain temple in China where iron-glazed bowls were used for tea."
steps.native: A Song Jian-ware tenmoku bowl: a deep conical wheel-thrown bowl of dense dark stoneware, thickly glazed brown-black with a glossy running glaze that pools in a dark bead above the foot, pale hare's-fur streaks and a rust-brown rim; set on a black lacquer stand with a flared foot, shown alone and centred, nothing else on the surface. Precise, glossy, sumptuous: the thing wabi tea replied to.

note: English Wikipedia says Ikkyū gave Jukō a scroll by Yuanwu as proof of enlightenment; Japanese Wikipedia says that comes from the Nampōroku (a text suspected of being a forgery), that only four bowls appear as Jukō's in the earliest inventory, and that the later Jukō possessions (Yuanwu's scroll, Xu Xi's egret painting) may have been added. I dropped those, and anything that would need Japanese script.
confidence: Step 1 strong (Omotesenke itself, plus Wikipedia). Step 2 good by lineage; 'the craft from Jōō, the Way from Jukō' is attributed to Rikyū and the bowl purchase comes from tea records via Wikipedia. Step 3 is weakest: the tenmoku is what wabi tea answered, but I found no Rikyū sentence naming it.

name: Maynard

card.essence: the evening the money is for: money and machinery only the means, the point a good life with friends, beauty and talk. One small plump bird at ease.
rhymes: one small plump bird, only where a tradition natively makes one (a manuscript margin, the owl of Athens, the duck weight of Ur)
a measure kept honest (a weight, a coin, a count)
leave: the Omega Workshops manner: bold brushed outlines and flat blocks of colour, the Bloomsbury painters' style
any likeness, voice or endorsement of Keynes; no cash box or ledger as his emblem

step0.title: Maynard, as he is
step0.medium: Brushed oil or gouache on a plain wooden panel in the Omega Workshops manner: a plump songbird in bold flat colours

steps.title: after the Schoolmen on usury
steps.medium: Ink and pigment on vellum: a scholastic manuscript of Aquinas's Summa theologiae (II-II, question 78, 'on the sin of usury')
steps.link: Keynes read the medieval doctors' fight over interest as an honest intellectual effort, and in 1930 called for a return to the old 'traditional virtue' that avarice is a vice and usury a misdemeanour. He does not name Aquinas; I use the Summa as the standard text they all began from.
steps.source: Keynes, General Theory (1936), ch. 23: "I was brought up to believe that the attitude of the Medieval Church to the rate of interest was inherently absurd ... But I now read these discussions as an honest intellectual effort to keep separate what the classical theory has inextricably confused together, namely, the rate of interest and the marginal efficiency of capital." Keynes, 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren' (1930): "I see us free, therefore, to return to some of the most sure and certain principles of religion and traditional virtue - that avarice is a vice, that the exaction of usury is a misdemeanour, and the love of money is detestable ... We shall once more value ends above means and prefer the good to the useful."
steps.native: A late-13th-century scholastic manuscript such as Bruges Public Library MS 563 (the Secunda secundae): two columns of tiny black Gothic textura on ruled vellum, red rubrics, red-and-blue pen-flourished initials, one decorated initial at the head of the question on usury, wide margins with a few small birds and leaf sprays drawn by the rubricator. Dense, plain and exact; the one decorated letter is the only gesture.

steps.title: after Aristotle's money
steps.link: Aquinas builds his teaching on usury on Aristotle, citing the Politics and the Ethics by name; Aristotle's own line that money 'exists not by nature but by law' is the old form of the state-money idea Keynes adopts in the Treatise. Keynes is not recorded citing it there (UNCONFIRMED).
steps.source: Aquinas, ST II-II q.78 a.1: "Now money, according to the Philosopher (Ethic. v, 5; Polit. i, 3) was invented chiefly for the purpose of exchange". Aristotle, Nic. Ethics V.5 (Ross): "money has become by convention a sort of representative of demand; and this is why it has the name 'money' (nomisma)-because it exists not by nature but by law (nomos) and it is in our power to change it and make it useless." Ethics I.5: "wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else." Coin type: Agora Excavations N 24585.
steps.native: A silver tetradrachm of classical Athens, about 24 mm and 17 g, a thick, slightly irregular flan struck between two dies: on one face the helmeted head of Athena in profile with olive leaves on her helmet, on the other a plump owl standing and facing us, with an olive spray, a crescent and the letters ΑΘΕ; toned grey, a little worn at the edges. The bird is the whole value of the thing.

steps.title: after the duck weights of Ur
steps.medium: Polished dark stone: a duck-shaped weight with a short cuneiform inscription
steps.date: Ur or Nippur, c. 2100-2000 BC (Third Dynasty of Ur, Shulgi)
steps.kind: tradition (borrowed word and weight system); spiritual as to intent
steps.link: Keynes puts the first state-fixed standard of weight in Babylonia 'towards the end of the third millennium B.C.'; the Greek mina (mna) is a word borrowed from Semitic and the Attic talent is 60 minae, as in Mesopotamia. The Shulgi-era duck weights are the surviving objects of that reform (Keynes does not name them; UNCONFIRMED that he meant it).
steps.source: Keynes, Treatise on Money, vol. 1 (1930), ch. 1: "The first State reform of the standard of weight, of which we have definite record, was the Babylonian reform towards the end of the third millennium B.C." Wikipedia, Mina (unit): "The Greek word mna was borrowed from Semitic." Mainz University on a Shulgi duck weight: stone, 5 ma-na (about 2,500 g), actual weight 2,478 g, inscription tying the standard to the king.
steps.native: An Ur III state weight: a smooth, dark, polished stone (diorite or pyroxenite) carved as a plump duck resting with its neck turned back along its body, the underside flat so it sits true, a short line of cuneiform incised on the back naming the king and the weight in minas. No paint, no ornament, fitted to the hand. A bird that is the standard.

note: Marshall as teacher is documented (the New Palgrave life lists Keynes among his pupils, and Marshall steered him into economics), but Marshall's own debts in the 1890 preface (Cournot, von Thünen) are books and diagrams, so that line would be one medium three times; I left it out for the medium rule. Moore's Principia Ethica (1903), the book Keynes says dominated his circle, says the charter's idea almost in words: "By far the most valuable things ... are certain states of consciousness, which may be roughly described as the pleasures of human intercourse and the enjoyment of beautiful objects" (s.113); Moore cites Plato's Philebus. A Moore-Plato line is the best alternative if you prefer ideas to money. The 'Babylonian madness' phrase for Keynes's 1920s ancient-currency study reached me only second-hand (NYT review quoted by E-Sylum), so not used.
confidence: Step 1: Keynes's approval of the Schoolmen is in his own words, but he never names Aquinas. Step 2: Aquinas citing Aristotle is solid; Keynes citing Aristotle is not shown. Step 3 is the weakest: Keynes names Babylon, not Ur or duck weights, and the Babylon-to-Athens hand-off is a borrowed word and a weight system, not a documented transmission.
